SCMP: "After blanketing the country in railways, expressways, airports and seagoing canals to reach a 91 per cent completion rate, the push for the next 4 percentage points raises questions for the world’s second-largest economy: what’s left to build, and how are massive projects being justified when the nation’s most economically vibrant regions are already connected?"

The answer, of course, is that the rush to expand the country's transportation system has much less to do with the economic benefits of an expanded transportation system and much more to do with the need to shift investment out of China's already-excessive investment in manufacturing, which was itself the result of the need to shift investment out of China's excessive investment in property.

Since the contraction in China's trade surplus after the GFC, Beijing's consistent strategy has been to shift investment into another sector whenever excess capacity and debt has made the previous sector unsustainable.

But with property investment, infrastructure investment, and manufacturing investment already excessive, and the country's debt burden rising so quickly, it takes more and more imagination to find a new area of investment that can be justified.

Quick takes:
- We should not punish companies for these kinds of disclosures, reputationally or otherwise (e.g. non-useful red tape parallel enquiries). They are important, and you don't punish companies for behaviour you want to keep seeing.

- We are seeing this from Anthropic and OpenAI for 2 reasons
i) because they are ahead on capabilities
ii) because they do the kinds of demanding cybersecurity evaluations that are really important to do in order to understand these capabilities and risks.
This is an industry/technology problem, not a company problem

- If xAI were a little further ahead with their massive training run plans, we would be seeing even more chaotic outcomes. Ditto the up and coming Chinese competitors - they simply don't have the headcount on non-capability tasks to be monitoring as closely as OAI/Anthr were, and OAI/Anthr's monitoring was insufficient.

- In 6-12 months open source models will have similar capabilities. Whether this leads to widespread problems turns on your views on the following
1) Whether equivalently powerful open source models can effectively be used to defend, the world over, and whether orgs have the skills to use them sufficiently well. and
2) Whether more advanced closed source models can defend orgs sufficiently widely, and whether orgs can afford to use them (or are given access).
I am concerned.

- It is quite plausible, perhaps even likely, that at some point we'll see a scenario such as a US model 'seeking its cyber eval answers' within the infrastructure of a Chinese company, or something equivalent. BEFORE that happens, we need better communication channel, trusted incident-sharing, trusted intermediaries, and de-escalation pathways.

Yes, we are past the point of no return.

When debt service payments squeeze out spending, it is like plaque in the circulatory system squeezing out the flow of blood. It is the same kind of thing, and it can be measured. We are seeing that happen right now.

There is also a supply and demand issue. A budget deficit means that debt has to be sold. We can see this happening in the bond market—bonds have been a bad investment, and there is pressure on interest rates and borrowing.

This dynamic is happening, but people are treating it like it hasn't happened before. They don't understand that, just like plaque in the arteries, the debt builds up and they have that exposure.

The @NYCMayor Mamdani pied a terre tax (the PAT tax) will likely reduce overall tax revenues for NY and that’s before considering the capital flight it will cause. 

When a NYC home is burdened with an additional annual tax, the home value will decline by the capitalized value of that new tax. 

While the PAT tax is set at 5%, it is 5% of the assessed value of the home, which is generally substantially less than its market value.  Assessed values are typically a fraction, let’s say 6%-15%, of the market value of a home and/or apartment so economically the PAT tax should be approximately 0.3%-0.75% of the market value of the home. 

Using a 4% cap rate, a 0.3%-0.75% PAT tax should reduce market values and annual real estate tax collections by 7.5%-18.75% assuming people believe the tax will be payable annually over the long term. 

The impact on current real estate values is not just on owners whose primary residence is elsewhere. As such, the value of all NYC residential real estate is going to decline. This will lead to substantially reduced assessed values and lower overall real estate tax collections. 

And all of the above is before considering capital flight as more wealthy NYers leave the city and the desirability of NYC residential real estate declines. 

Tell me why I am wrong.
@FiftySeth @NYCMayor You’re missing the point. The purpose of the tax is to raise revenues. It is going to cause overall real estate tax revenues to decline.
